extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic/philosophy (readers of a classical logic treatise)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions and classificatory criteria for kinds of names (abstract/concrete, connotative/non-connotative, relative, privative, etc.) used in logic and philosophy of language, with guidance on usage, examples, and pitfalls. Useful for someone formalizing or teaching the semantics of naming and predication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract vs. concrete names
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract = the name of an attribute; concrete = the name of an object. (Author adopts the older schoolmen sense: 'By abstract ... I shall always, in Logic proper, mean the opposite of concrete; by an abstract name, the name of an attribute; by a concrete name, the name of an object.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'abstract' to denote attribute-names (e.g., whiteness) and 'concrete' for object-names (e.g., man). Note historical confusion: modern usage sometimes misapplies 'abstract' to all general names—avoid that misuse. Examples and discussion: 'whiteness' vs 'white', 'man' as concrete name of many objects, 'humanity' as name of attribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: General vs. singular status of abstract names
rubrics_metrics.description: Some abstract names are general (name a class of attributes, e.g., color, magnitude, weight); others name a single attribute (e.g., visibleness, milk-whiteness) and thus are neither properly general nor individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an abstract denotes several varying instances (different shades/degrees) treat it as general; when it designates one determinate attribute (no degree/kind variation) consider placing it in a separate class rather than forcing it into 'general' or 'individual'. Examples: 'color' (general) vs 'milk-whiteness' (neither general nor individual).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal use / predicative meaning determines a word's name-role
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider a word as the name of what it is intended to be understood as in its principal use (especially in predication). Thus 'white' is a name of white things (subjects), while 'whiteness' is the name of the color (attribute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between words that 'stand for' attributes vs those that are predicated of subjects. Avoid conflating adjectival use with abstract-noun use; examine the principal predicative employment to decide what a word names. Example: when saying 'snow is white' we mean snow has a color, not that snow is the color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotative vs. non-connotative names (denotation vs. connotation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-connotative terms signify a subject only or an attribute only (e.g., John, whiteness). Connotative terms denote a subject and imply (connote) an attribute (e.g., white, virtuous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to analyze the informational content of names: connotative names not only pick out subjects but also communicate (connote) attributes. All concrete general names are connotative. Examples: 'white' denotes white things and connotes whiteness; 'man' denotes individuals and connotes attributes like corporeity, rationality, human form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names are non-connotative
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper names denote the individual only and do not imply any attributes as part of their signification (e.g., Paul, Dartmouth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not read attribute-claims into proper names; any association (e.g., Dartmouth = at mouth of Dart) is contingent to historical naming and not part of the name's meaning. Proper names function as distinguishing marks for discourse, not as carriers of descriptive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotative individual names (individuals named by connotation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual names can be connotative when the meaning of the name itself implies attributes such that only one individual fits (e.g., 'the only son of John Stiles', 'the first emperor of Rome').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that an apparently individual name may connote attributes (uniqueness, relation to events) that make it effectively connotative. Contextual modifiers (articles, adjectives) can individualize otherwise general connotative names (e.g., 'the present prime minister of England').

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning resides chiefly in connotation rather than denotation
rubrics_metrics.description: When names convey information, that information typically resides in what they connote (the attributes implied), not merely in the set of things they denote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To understand a name's meaning, determine the connotation (attributes it implies). Knowing all individuals a name can be affirmed of (denotation) does not suffice to know the name's meaning. Example: many different names (Sophroniscus, father of Socrates, man, Greek) denote the same individual but carry different connotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indeterminate connotation and its dangers
rubrics_metrics.description: Some general names have vague or unsettled connotations (e.g., 'man' — how much deviation from human form or how little rationality still counts?). This indeterminacy can cause vague thinking unless guarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a name's connotation is indeterminate, adopt strict precautions: give definite, fixed connotations to frequently used general concrete names to avoid lax habits of thought. The philosopher's task is to fix connotation with minimal disruption to ordinary usage and truth of common propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple fixed connotations (ambiguity) vs. indeterminate connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish words with several fixed and recognized meanings (ambiguous/æquivocal) from names whose connotation is indeterminate and lacks a precise accepted sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ambiguous word can be treated as multiple names (different senses) provided the senses are clearly distinguished; indeterminate connotation requires analytic definition or precision rather than merely noting multiple senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive vs. negative names
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive names (man, tree, good) name presence of attributes; negative names (not-man, not-tree, not-good) name absence of attributes. Every positive concrete name may have a corresponding negative name denoting everything except that class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that negative names connote absence of an attribute (non-possession is itself an attribute). Also be aware that form and reality may diverge: words positive in form can be negative in reality (e.g., 'idle' = 'not working'), and words negative in form can express positive attributes (e.g., 'inconvenient').

rubrics_metrics.name: Privative names
rubrics_metrics.description: Privative names are equivalent to a positive and a negative taken together: they name something that once had an attribute or might have been expected to have it, but does not (e.g., 'blind').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privative terms connote both absence of a particular attribute and presence of other attributes from which the absence would be noteworthy. Avoid equating privative words with a simple negation ('blind' ≠ 'not seeing' in many uses). Consider social/expectational context in analysis (e.g., applied to beings expected to see).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative (relational) vs. non-relative names
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative names (father, son, cause, effect, longer, shorter) always come in pairs and, when predicated, imply the existence of another object (their correlative). A relative name's attribute is a relation founded on a series of facts involving two or more objects—the fundamentum relationis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing relative names, identify the underlying fact/series of events they both express in different modes (e.g., 'A is father of B' and 'B is son of A' express the same fact). Define the relation by the events that constitute it. Use this to explain how relative connotation differs from other attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Univocal, æquivocal (ambiguous), and analogical/metaphorical application of names
rubrics_metrics.description: Univocal application: a name used in the same sense for all instances. Æquivocal/ambiguous: a name used in different senses for different instances (effectively different names that happen to coincide in sound). Analogical/metaphorical: intermediate case where the name is used in a derived, similar but not identical sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ambiguous words as distinct names with distinct meanings when senses are distinct. Beware of the fallacy of taking a metaphorical/analogical use as if it were literal/univocal—that is a common source of fallacious reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixing connotation via definition to promote precise thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving a fixed connotation to a general concrete name (by definition or analysis) is the proper remedy for indeterminate connotation, aiming to change usage minimally while improving precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining in order to fix connotation, aim for least possible change in the objects the name habitually denotes and minimal disruption of commonly accepted true propositions. Recognize that some vagueness may be pragmatically beneficial (e.g., classification in natural history) but must be guarded by explicit criteria when precision is required.
